cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Name Your Backers
cards.instruction: Get someone to reveal who supports their position, who authorized it, and who benefits from it.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Before I tell the workshop staff they're closing, who backed your decision?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: The director approved it. Please just send the notice.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. I'll name her approval. Who else supported it?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Sales. They're getting the floor space, but leave them out.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Then Sales can join the staff meeting. Who signed off on giving them our space?

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 asserts control and A5 orders Sales attendance, but A3 naming approval is mostly investigative cooperation rather than status-specific handling of B request.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 director approval prompts A3 other supporters; B4 Sales benefit prompts A5 authorization of space transfer, a coherent expanding map.

relationship.evidence: B2 wants the notice sent and B4 wants beneficiaries left out, giving a credible motive for selective disclosure.

heightening.evidence: B4 identifies a benefiting department, so A5 turns hidden support into meeting attendance and a new approval question.

specificity.evidence: A1 workshop closure and B4 floor-space transfer define concrete consequences without requiring organizational history.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 Sales can attend is pointed; A3 stock decision prefix remains detachable and costly.
